name: Mobile developer
summary: Mobile developer interviews usually go deep on one platform (Android with Kotlin, iOS with Swift, or a cross-platform framework such as Flutter or React Native) and on how apps behave on real devices: lifecycles, memory, offline use and slow networks. Candidates commonly report a coding round or a take-home building a small app, and for experienced roles, questions on app architecture and releasing through the app stores.
rounds: Coding test or take-home: often a small app that loads data from an API and shows it
Platform interview: lifecycle, UI, threading, storage and the platform's own tools
Coding or problem-solving interview, sometimes general rather than mobile-specific
App architecture or design discussion for experienced roles
looks_for: Depth in one platform's lifecycle and UI toolkit
Keeping the main thread free so the app stays responsive
Handling offline use, poor networks and the app being restarted
A clear architecture that separates UI, state and data
Care with battery, memory and app size
Experience shipping and supporting an app in the stores

questions.text: Tell me about a crash that reached users. How did you find the cause and fix it?
covers: How you learned of it: crash reports, store reviews, support tickets
How you reproduced it: device, OS version, the exact steps
The fix, how you got it out quickly, and how you prevented similar crashes

questions.text: Describe a time you had to support older devices or OS versions while adding a new feature.
covers: The constraint and how many users it affected
How you handled it: fallbacks, version checks, raising the minimum version
The trade-off you agreed with the team

questions.text: Tell me about a release that didn't go to plan, such as a store rejection or a broken update.
covers: What went wrong and how you found out
What you did to recover, and how quickly
What you changed in your release process: checks, staged rollouts, feature flags

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with a designer to make an app feel right on its platform.
covers: Where the design clashed with or followed the platform's conventions
How you agreed the changes
How users responded

questions.text: Explain the lifecycle of an Android Activity or an iOS view controller, and a bug that comes from getting it wrong.
covers: The main states, and when the system creates, pauses or destroys a screen
Saving and restoring state, such as on an Android rotation or when the system ends the app in the background
A bug example: work continuing after the screen has gone, or lost user input

questions.text: Why must network and disk work stay off the main thread, and how do you do that on your platform?
covers: The main thread draws the UI; blocking it causes freezes and 'not responding' errors
Coroutines, Swift concurrency, Dart futures or background queues
Returning results to the main thread safely, and cancelling work when a screen closes

questions.text: How would you make an app work well offline and sync when the connection returns?
covers: A local database as the source the UI reads from
Queueing changes made offline and sending them later
Handling conflicts when the same data changed on the server meanwhile

questions.text: Your app's memory use keeps climbing as users move between screens. How would you find out why?
covers: Using the platform's memory profiler to see which objects stay alive
Common causes: listeners never removed, references to closed screens, oversized images
Fixing it and checking the memory graph again

questions.text: Compare architecture patterns such as MVVM and MVI. Which do you use, and why?
covers: What each separates: UI, state, logic and data
How the pattern makes testing and changes easier
An example from your own app, and the pattern's downsides

questions.text: How would you show a long, scrolling list of images smoothly?
covers: Lists that only build visible rows, such as RecyclerView, LazyColumn, UICollectionView or Flutter's ListView.builder
Loading and caching images at the right size, off the main thread
Placeholders, and cancelling loads for rows that scroll away

questions.text: Native or cross-platform: how would you choose for a new app?
covers: Team skills, time to market and the value of one codebase
Performance, access to platform features, and how native it must feel
Your own experience of the trade-offs

questions.text: How would you store a user's login token securely on the device?
covers: The Keychain on iOS and Keystore-backed storage on Android, not plain preferences
Short-lived tokens with refresh, cleared on logout
Never logging tokens or shipping secrets inside the app

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd set up push notifications that open the right screen in the app.
covers: Registering the device token with your server and keeping it current
Deep links, and handling the app being closed, in the background or open
Asking for permission at a sensible moment and not over-sending

questions.text: Users say the app takes too long to open. How would you investigate and speed up start-up?
covers: Measuring cold and warm start times on a mid-range device
Delaying work that the first screen doesn't need
A lighter first screen, fewer libraries set up at launch, and measuring again

questions.text: How do you test a mobile app, and what do you test on physical devices rather than emulators?
covers: Unit tests for logic and UI tests for the key flows
Physical devices for performance, camera, sensors, push and different screen sizes
Beta testing and staged rollouts before a full release

questions.text: Why mobile development? Which app do you admire, and why?
covers: What draws you to mobile: building for the device in people's hands, the craft, the platform
A specific app and one detail it gets right
Something you'd like to build

questions.text: What would you improve first in our app, and how would you know it helped?
covers: A specific issue you noticed while using the app
The change and what it would cost to build
A metric such as ratings, crash-free sessions or retention

tips: Install and use the company's app before the interview; note one thing you like and one you'd improve.
Pick one platform and go deep; interviewers usually value real depth in Kotlin or Swift over a little of everything.
Keep an app you can demo on your phone or in the store, and know its architecture well.
When you describe any feature, mention what happens offline, on rotation or when the app is killed; those cases set strong answers apart.
Know your platform's profiling tools by name and what you've used them to find.
